subject: truck2077
pitch:
Category: Vehicle.
Subject: futuristic militarized truck from 2077.
Style: low-poly cyberpunk, extremely intricate.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a single TypeScript module to build a low-poly cyberpunk military truck using the SDK's known builder APIs, favoring static parts with basic geometry, extrusion, and paneling techniques to keep it runnable.

For the look, I'm thinking gunmetal panel paint with hazard stripes plus neon cyan/magenta accents from a glow kit, structuring the truck as a cab up front and cargo box behind, roughly 6.5m long with six wheels across three axles, all parented to the root since no joints are strictly needed for a static model.

Planning out z-coordinate ranges for the cab, hood, and cargo box while keeping wheels centered at the right height for the 0.55m radius, then setting up wheel cylinders rotated to spin along the X axis via the dir parameter.

I'm thinking through paint treatments next — panelled armor plating for the hull, metallic finishes, glowing neon underglow strips and headlights, and hazard stripe patterns driven by position-based coloring functions. Then I start laying out the actual chassis rails, wheel assemblies with tires, hubs, and bolts, building each piece as layered cylinder geometries.

I'm working out wheel placement along the chassis and considering fender arches above them, deciding box-shaped fenders are simpler than curved cylinder arcs. Now I'm starting the cab structure, blocking out its dimensions and thinking about extruding a sloped windshield profile.

Defining extrusion profile points...

Positioning the glass planes correctly...

Now I'm planning the cargo box dimensions, hazard stripe panels, neon glow strips, and cyber details like the roof antenna array, rear ramp hatch, and turret mount.

I'm sketching out more surface details: a gun turret with rotated barrel, exhaust pipes, cyan underglow, glowing headlights and grille, a door emblem decal using a textured plane, and glowing rear cargo lights.

Now I'm planning the paint functions and textures: hazard stripe paint computed from diagonal position, metal/panelled finishes imported from the clockwork kit, glow effects from the glow kit, and tread grooves on the tires using angle-based masking — plus SVGs for the emblem, HUD, and "UNIT 77" cargo logo text.

I'm also sketching a small box-building helper function and a Fill type alias to keep the body/cargo geometry calls concise and typed consistently.

Writing builder setup code...

Setting up the glass paint shader, then starting the builder function with a box-helper utility for constructing the hull parts.

Now I'm designing texture assets: a cyber-styled emblem SVG with hexagon and stroke lines, a HUD overlay with arcs and a percentage readout, and a bold logo text texture for "WH-77" branding. Then I start laying out the chassis geometry, placing side rails, crossmembers, and an underside plate using the box-building helper with specific positions and dark coloring.

Still building the wheel assembly...

Now I'm shaping the cab using an extruded profile outline for the body, then adding glass window panels extruded along the sides with their own outline points.

I need to make sure the glass thickness and offset keep it positioned flush within the cab wall rather than poking outside it, so I'm nudging the glass center and thickness values to fit snugly against the 1.1 cab wall boundary.

For the windshield, I'm skipping a tilted box approach and instead building it as a flat extruded trapezoid outline in the XY plane, with the x and y basis vectors giving thickness along z so it sits flush against the front of the cab.

The slanted nose geometry makes a clean plane placement tricky since z varies with y along the slope, so I'll simplify by treating the windshield as glass side windows plus a grille of light bars on the front instead of trying to perfectly fit a tilted surface. I'm adding the cab roof as a flat box with a glowing light bar on top, then moving on to cab door details.

For the door, I'm placing a textured emblem decal on the side panel, adding thin dark seam lines around the door outline, and setting up glowing headlight boxes near the front nose with a dark grille strip accented by neon horizontal lights. I'm also sketching a front bumper box and considering spike-based bull bars using a spike helper that takes a base point, direction, length, and radius.

Now I'm working out the cargo box geometry, sizing it to bridge the gap behind the cab with a connector panel, then adding a roof rack, antenna spikes with glowing tips, and side panel logo decals sized to fit the cargo width.

Next I'm placing a hazard stripe band along the cargo side, neon glow strips in cyan and magenta running the length of the vehicle, and detailing the rear with a seamed door panel and red brake lights. I'm also starting to lathe a turret ring profile for the roof.

Still working out the gun turret and barrel geometry...

Checking if the skirt panel position overlaps the tire geometry, I'm adjusting its placement outward and raising it slightly to avoid clipping.

Then I'm skipping the cab wheel arches and focusing on cyber details instead—thin neon rod cables running from the cargo top to the antennas, plus a lathe-generated satellite dish mounted on the cargo roof. For the HUD display, since the cab interior isn't visible, I'm deciding to place it as a decal on the front grille instead.

Actually I'll move the HUD to the rear door as a status screen facing backward, with a glow effect applied so the colors pop. I'm adding hazard stripes to the cargo rear and bumper, spiked chrome studs across the front bumper, a license plate decal, and finishing with a greeble pass—scattering small boxes along the cargo sides for texture, bringing the total part count to roughly 100.

I'm double-checking the API signatures before finalizing: extrude needs an outline plus position, direction, and thickness; glow works directly on parts; lathe takes an axis vector; spike takes a base point, direction, length, and radius; rod takes two points and a radius before color. With these confirmed, I'm ready to write the final ~300 lines of code, making sure to drop any unused type imports along the way.

Setting up imports for the builder, color types, and the clockwork/glow kits, then moving into building SVG textures for emblem decals using layered polygons with cyan and magenta strokes.

Writing SVG code...

Now I'm planning the vehicle body geometry: wheels placed symmetrically along each axle with rubber tires, chrome hub cylinders, glowing neon caps, and bolt details arranged radially around each hub face.

Next I'm working through mudguards above the tires, then moving to the cab structure — roof panel, a glowing light bar near the windshield, and the side window glass shaped to follow the sloped nose profile so it fits flush against the hull.

I'm adding door seams, an emblem decal on the door, exhaust stacks, and a connector box joining the cab to the cargo section before building the cargo body itself with its top rail and roof rack greebles.

Now I'm layering on surface detail for the cargo box: a hazard band near the base, glowing neon strips, a logo decal plane on the side, and scattered rivet-like greeble boxes with randomized placement and colors. I'm also setting up the rear door seam and a HUD-style decal plane, adjusting position so it doesn't collide with the seam line.

I'm moving to the rear bumper and lighting now—glowing red taillights, a dark bumper box, and a hazard stripe along it—then shifting to the front end with a grille, alternating glowing slats, bright headlight glows, and a matching front bumper with its own hazard strip and spike details along the bottom edge.

Now I'm designing the roof turret on the cargo deck: a lathe-profile ring base, a boxy gunmetal head sitting atop it, and a forward-pointing barrel with a muzzle brake, working out the coordinates so the barrel properly extends from the turret head.

Next I'm adding roof antennas with glowing tips, a satellite dish lathe shape, cable rods strung along the roof, an underglow strip beneath the chassis, and side skirts near the wheel wells, adjusting positions so these elements don't awkwardly clip through the tires.

I'm also adding small chrome door handles, a chassis rail, and some rear greeble details, then finalizing the structure with the default export and making sure parts without joints attach properly to the root — aiming for a complete, reasonably concise script around 230 lines.
